strengths: Introduces a practical and well-motivated idea: amortizing the uncertainty estimation for active view selection into a single lightweight feedforward network (UPNet), eliminating the need to iteratively retrain per-scene NeRF/3DGS models at inference time. This yields substantial efficiency gains (up to 400x speedup, >50% reduction in CPU/RAM/GPU usage) which is a meaningful practical contribution.

Reasonably thorough experimental protocol: evaluation under both in-domain (ID) and out-of-domain (OOD; novel category) settings, with three types of metrics (image quality, mesh quality, visual coverage), and cross-validation with two different downstream neural rendering models (NeRF and 3DGS) to test generalization of selected viewpoints.
Contributes a sizable new dataset (NUM: 62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs across 13 ShapeNet categories, computed with 4 different uncertainty metrics) that could be a useful resource for the community.

Includes a decent set of ablations (uncertainty metric choice, redundancy-removal and aggregation strategies, instance-diversity vs. viewpoint-density trade-off) that provide some insight into design choices.

The interpolation-based aggregation scheme allows selection over an arbitrary (non-fixed) candidate set, addressing a limitation of prior learning-based NBV methods that rely on discrete candidate sets.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted entirely to synthetic, single, centered ShapeNet objects with a fixed spherical viewpoint distribution; no real-world or cluttered/multi-object scene evaluation is provided, which substantially limits the demonstrated scope of the claimed generalization (this limitation is acknowledged by the authors but not empirically probed).

Accuracy gains over the strongest baseline (NVF) are quite modest in the ID setting (e.g., PSNR 33.19 vs. 33.08, mesh Acc. 0.35 vs 0.36, nearly tied CR), suggesting the primary advantage of the method is computational efficiency rather than reconstruction quality; the gap to the Upper-bound (36.47 vs 33.19 PSNR, ~3dB) is still fairly large, weakening the "comparable to upper bound" claim.
OOD generalization is tested on only 2 held-out categories (10 instances each), a very small and potentially unrepresentative sample for claims of generalization to "novel object categories."

The paper does not compare against recently cited 3DGS-based active view/mapping methods (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER) that are discussed in related work as directly competitive, leaving open whether PUN's gains hold against more modern baselines.

The ground-truth uncertainty used to supervise UPNet is a heuristic proxy (reconstruction error of a single-view synthesis model, Splatter-Image) rather than a principled measure of epistemic/geometric uncertainty; how well this proxy transfers to genuinely novel geometries or non-symmetric objects is not rigorously analyzed (the discussion of symmetry bias in Fig. 3 is speculative and only illustrated on 2 examples).

No qualitative visualizations of actual final 3D reconstructions (only uncertainty maps) are shown, making it hard to assess practical differences in reconstruction quality/failure modes between PUN and baselines.
Limited sensitivity analysis on some key hyperparameters (e.g., 512 candidate viewpoints, redundancy threshold of 0.1, 30° interpolation neighborhood) beyond the specific ablations reported.
Some claims (e.g., 'PUN performs on par with Upper-bnd') are somewhat overstated relative to the actual numeric gaps reported in the tables.

strengths: Novel and practical idea: predicting an uncertainty map directly from a single current-view image via a lightweight feedforward network (UPNet), avoiding costly per-step NeRF/3DGS retraining required by prior AVS methods.

Strong efficiency gains are convincingly demonstrated: up to 400x speedup and >50% reduction in CPU/RAM/GPU usage compared to baselines (Table S4), which is a meaningful practical contribution for real-time or resource-constrained AVS.
Large new dataset (NUM) with 62,400 viewpoint-UMap pairs across 13 categories is a useful contribution to the community and enables the proposed learning-based approach.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across 6 datasets/settings (novel instances, novel categories, lighting changes, camera distance changes, NeRFAssets, MIP360) and multiple reconstruction backbones (NeRF, 3DGS, Binocular3DGS), showing consistent gains over baselines.
Extensive ablations (uncertainty metric choice, viewpoint selection policy, dataset diversity vs. density, anchor number, redundancy threshold) provide useful insight into design choices.

Interesting analysis (Sec 5.2) correlating UPNet's predicted uncertainty with generic geometric/texture complexity measures, offering some interpretability into why the method generalizes to unseen categories/backbones.
weaknesses: The ground-truth uncertainty maps are derived from a single fixed single-view synthesis backbone (Splatter-Image); this is a heuristic proxy for 'true' reconstruction uncertainty for multi-view training, and while the paper offers a plausible correlation argument (Fig S4, r=0.82) and complexity-metric analysis, the link between single-view synthesis error and downstream multi-view NeRF/3DGS reconstruction difficulty is not rigorously established.

The paper omits direct empirical comparison to several closely related and recent 3DGS-based AVS methods discussed extensively in the related work (ActiveSplat, ActiveGS, ActiveGAMER), which seems like a significant gap given these are the most comparable recent approaches leveraging density/geometry cues.

Reported standard deviations in several tables (e.g., Table S1 NUM-cat) are large and often overlap between PUN and the next-best baseline (e.g., NVF), raising questions about the statistical significance of some of the claimed improvements.

Absolute performance on the real-world MIP360 dataset remains quite low (PSNR ~15-17, SSIM ~0.2-0.3), suggesting limited practical transfer to complex real scenes despite the method's synthetic-domain effectiveness; the gains over NVF, while present, are on a weak overall baseline.

The next-viewpoint selection heuristic (redundancy filtering via a fixed threshold, plus multiplicative aggregation of interpolated uncertainties across timesteps) is somewhat ad hoc, and its sensitivity/robustness across truly diverse scene types (vs. single centered objects) is unclear.

The method assumes a spherical viewpoint distribution around a single, centered object; this restricts applicability to more general, unconstrained 3D environments or multi-object scenes, a limitation the authors acknowledge but do not address empirically.

Training data is entirely synthetic ShapeNet renders with limited category/instance diversity (13 categories, 100 instances each), which may limit generalization despite the reported cross-domain tests.
